title: Foot cream: how to look after dry, rough feet at home
body:
Feet have thicker skin than the rest of the body and few oil glands, so they are often the first place to feel dry, especially in winter, when boots, tights and central heating all take their toll. A good foot cream, used regularly, keeps heels and soles feeling soft and comfortable. Here is how to choose one, and how to fit it into a simple at-home pedicure.

Why feet get so dry

The skin on your heels and soles takes your weight all day. It is naturally thick, and when it dries out it can feel rough and tight. Hot baths, long showers, walking barefoot on hard floors and closed shoes in heated rooms all make it drier. Moisturising little and often works better than an occasional rescue.

Foot cream or foot butter?

  • A foot cream contains water as well as oils and butters, so it sinks in quickly. It suits daily use, morning or night.
  • A foot butter or balm has no water: it is a solid blend of oils, butters and wax that sits on the skin for longer. It suits very dry heels and works well at night under cotton socks.

Foot cream: Vilvah Foot Care Cream

Vilvah Foot Care Cream (£16, 100ml) is a rich cream with four butters (shea, avocado, mango and cocoa), sunflower, argan and kalonji (black seed) oils, glycerine and a little peppermint oil for a cool, fresh scent. Massage it into clean, dry feet, ideally before bed. It also comes as the Vilvah Foot Cream & Body Lotion Kit (£37.99), paired with the Milk Body Lotion (oat milk, ceramide, olive squalane and jojoba oil) for the rest of the body.

Foot butter: Deyga Foot Butter

Deyga Foot Butter (£12.99, 40g) is a short-ingredient balm: virgin coconut oil, olive oil, refined beeswax, vitamin E and vanilla essential oil. Warm a little between your fingers and work it into heels, soles and toes. For a richer finish, put it on at night and slip on cotton socks. It contains beeswax, so it is not vegan.

Already have a favourite body butter? A rich one such as Deyga Rose & Geranium Body Butter (£15.99) works on feet too; our body butter guide explains how to use it.

A simple at-home pedicure

  1. Soak. Dissolve two spoonfuls of Deyga Foot Soak Powder (£16.99, 160g) in a bowl of warm water. It blends sea salt and Himalayan pink salt with rose, lemon and peppermint oil. Soak for 10 to 15 minutes, no longer.
  2. Scrub. Massage Deyga Foot Scrub (£17.99, 100g) over damp feet in slow circles, focusing on the heels. Granulated sugar gives it a gentle grit, in coconut and almond oils with shea butter. Rinse with warm water. Once or twice a week is enough.
  3. Dry well, especially between the toes.
  4. Moisturise with foot cream or foot butter, then put on clean cotton socks if it is bedtime.

The Deyga Mini Foot Spa Combo (£35.99) puts the soak, the scrub and the foot butter in one box, which also makes an easy Christmas present. A natural Deyga Organic Loofah (£12.99) is handy for a quick buff of the heels in the shower. For scrubs for the rest of the body, see our body scrub guide.

Everyday habits for comfortable feet

  • Moisturise daily, ideally after a bath or shower, while skin is still slightly damp.
  • Keep showers warm, not hot, and do not leave feet soaking for long.
  • Wear socks around the house in winter rather than walking barefoot on cold, hard floors.
  • Do not use foot cream between the toes; keep that skin dry.

Good to know

  • Patch test before first use: the cream, butter and soak all contain essential oils, and the scrub contains almond oil.
  • Do not scrub broken or sore skin.
  • If you have diabetes or poor circulation, ask your GP or a podiatrist before soaking or scrubbing your feet.
  • Painful, deep or bleeding cracks in the heels, or any change you are unsure about, are worth showing to a pharmacist, your GP or a podiatrist.

summary: Foot cream, foot butter, scrub or soak: what each one does, a simple at-home pedicure, and how to keep dry feet comfortable through winter.
